title: The scribe of the Granth
hook: a man writes out the Guru's hymns word for word, and keeps his own poems beside the book

segments.voice: Yesterday, year two closed, and your line was the day, in his words. Were the last words you heard last night the Guru's? Year three starts now. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

One man reads a hymn aloud, slowly. Another dips his pen, writes down every word, and waits for the next line. Sikh tradition remembers a scene like that: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, gathering the hymns of the Gurus before him, and a learned Sikh named Bhai Gurdas writing them out into one great volume, the Adi Granth. Year three is the long story, Sikh history told slowly. And every long story needs someone who writes things down. Today: the scribe of the Granth.
screen: `ONE MAN READS.` → `ANOTHER WRITES EVERY WORD.` → `THE LONG STORY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Who was he? Tradition remembers Bhai Gurdas as a relative of the third Guru, Guru Amar Das. Tradition also says he grew up close to the Gurus' household, with the hymns around him. When Guru Arjan gathered the Guru's word into one book, tradition says Bhai Gurdas was the one holding the pen while the Guru dictated. It's a strange and humble job. Your hand moves, but the words aren't yours. A scribe who adds a flourish of his own, or fixes a line he'd have written differently, has failed at the one thing a scribe is for. The whole skill is faithfulness. Now the twist. This same man was a poet with a voice of his own. He composed vars, Punjabi ballads, about the Gurus and the Sikh way of life. And he did not slip them into the volume he was writing out. His vars stand beside the Granth, never inside it. He knew exactly which words were the Guru's and which were his, and he never blurred the line. Sikhs still sing his work. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the community's code of conduct, names the writings of Bhai Gurdas among those that may be sung as kirtan in the gurdwara, alongside gurbani, the Guru's own word. So the scribe's voice still sounds in the room, next to the book he copied, and never mistaken for it. And here's why year three begins with him. Bhai Gurdas is also a teller of the Sikh story. His first var tells of Guru Nanak's life and travels. Over the coming days, we'll walk through that var.
screen: `A RELATIVE OF GURU AMAR DAS.` · `THE SCRIBE: FAITHFUL HANDS.` · `THE POET: HIS VARS BESIDE THE GRANTH.` · `A TELLER OF THE STORY.` · then, large: `THE SCRIBE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line by hand, carefully. Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Choose a line you know: the line you kept from last year, a line of the Mool Mantar, or just one word, Waheguru. Write it slowly, letter by letter, as if the page might outlast you. Don't add anything. Don't decorate it. When it's finished, read it back once and check every word against the original. That's the scribe's whole craft: care, and nothing of your own slipped in. If you pray, you can say the line under your breath as you write. The bell holds the time.
The scribe of the Granth. Bhai Gurdas, who, tradition says, wrote out the Adi Granth for Guru Arjan, and whose own vars Sikhs still sing beside it.
screen: `THE SCRIBE OF THE GRANTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the scribe. Today, when you pass on someone else's words, a message, a recipe, a quote, pass them on exactly, with no spin of your own. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

screen: `DAY 697 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE KEY TO THE GRANTH.`

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Gurdas as the scribe of the Adi Granth, and his vars are sung and explained in gurdwaras alongside gurbani, though they are not part of the Guru Granth Sahib.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scribe is just a copier.
what it means: Bhai Gurdas wrote out the Guru's words faithfully and kept his own poems apart from them.
what a scholar hears: the Rehat Maryada lets his writings be sung in the gurdwara with gurbani, so the scribe's own voice still sounds beside the book.
